claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure consisting of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated starting alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and exhibits brittleness.
The untreated alloy develops significant dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries during tensile deformation.
Dislocation pile-ups at the internal boundaries cause local stress concentrations.
Boundary-associated dislocation pile-ups and stress concentrations lead to microcracking and brittle fracture under tension.
Room-temperature rolling or high-pressure torsion can be localized selectively near internal colony interfaces.
Localized severe plastic deformation followed by annealing at approximately 0.3–0.4 Tm will form a continuous nanocrystalline layer along internal phase boundaries.
Annealing at approximately 0.3–0.4 Tm will relieve residual stresses while retaining the interfacial nanostructure.
Nanocrystalline interfacial layers act as alternative dislocation sources.
Nanocrystalline interfacial layers act as dislocation sinks.
The source-and-sink behavior of the nanocrystalline layers redistributes plastic strain.
The nanocrystalline layers mitigate dislocation accumulation at conventional internal boundaries.
Redistributing plastic strain and reducing dislocation accumulation lowers local stress concentrations.
Lower local stress concentrations delay or prevent microcrack initiation under tensile loading.
The processed alloy will have greater room-temperature elongation to fracture than the untreated alloy.
The processed alloy will retain or slightly increase room-temperature yield strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The processed alloy will retain or slightly increase room-temperature ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The intervention will make the alloy more damage-tolerant and tougher during room-temperature tensile deformation.
